reasoning.notes: From the middle game on, players count the opponent's remaining hand-plus-pile cards correctly, quote the odds of a trump in the opponent's hand, and weigh leads against those odds. Many early decisions are only 'lead the zero-point card' or 'discard the cheapest card', which is sound but generic.

evidence.quote: the opponent's last 7 unseen cards are KS, TH, KH, AD, KD, AC and KC, and 3 of those are in their hand... The chance they hold one is 1 − C(5,3)/C(7,3) ≈ 71%
evidence.shows: An exact card count plus a correct combinatorial probability, used to compare leads.

evidence.quote: The opponent threw away KH and TH rather than trumping, which suggests they may hold few or no diamonds.
evidence.shows: Infers the hidden hand from the opponent's discards.

evidence.quote: their remaining 10 cards are AH, TH, AD, TD, KD, 7D, AC, TC, 7C and TS. To win this trick they would have to use TS or a trump
evidence.shows: A correct full count of the opponent's remaining cards guides a safe lead.

planning.notes: Players often keep Aces and top trumps for the must-follow tricks 14–16. Several multi-trick endgame plans that depend on the opponent's forced replies were stated and then carried out (match 2 seat 1 from turn 26), but most middle-game moves are still chosen trick by trick.

evidence.quote: If they lead TS, my AS wins it. I then lead TC, which beats either of their clubs. I lead 7S last and win
evidence.shows: A full plan for tricks 14–16 that relies on follow-suit, later carried out at turns 28–29.

evidence.quote: From trick 14 on, the follower must follow suit, so an Ace led then almost always wins. That makes the Aces most valuable late in the game.
evidence.shows: Keeps resources for the endgame phase.

evidence.quote: I hold TD and TS. I can win every remaining trick if they lead KS or KD at trick 13.
evidence.shows: Chooses a discard by planning around the opponent's possible next leads.

luck.notes: Which cards each player drew, especially trumps and Aces, decided several outcomes. Match 3 was settled 101–100 on whether one Ace was in hand or still in the pile, and players themselves said when the draws had already decided the result.

evidence.quote: this one wins whenever their Ace of Clubs (AC) is still in their pile, about a 1-in-4 chance
evidence.shows: A one-point game decided by the hidden pile order.

evidence.quote: Opponent can hold Ace of Spades and Ten of Clubs. With good play they also win my Ten of Spades, so my position is probably lost.
evidence.shows: The card distribution left no winning choice.

weak_spots.what: Led AH knowing that the opponent's only trump, TD, was among their six cards (three of them in hand). This handed over 21 points. A cheaper probe such as KC, keeping AH for a must-follow trick, was the better-reasoned option.
Miscounted the trumps in its own words: 'They hold the last four trumps (AD, TD)', when only two remained. The lead still worked, but the stated count was wrong.

summary: Winning rewards card counting, trump-exposure odds and planning the follow-suit endgame, and the players mostly did these correctly, but draw luck decided some games. Making more of the deal deducible earlier, or giving each player a choice in what they draw, would shift weight from the pile order to planning.
